title: Pitch Kitchen — Enterprise Demo Timing & Rebuttal Workshop
summary: Internal enablement rehearsal preparing the team for Acero Health pilot conversation. Focus on demo pacing (aiming for a 12-minute demo), tight segues between use cases, and rehearsing rebuttals for common enterprise objections: SOC 2/compliance, VPC/private deployment, latency vs cost tradeoffs, and data residency. Ran a dry 12-minute demo with time-checks and iterated on the closing ask.
topics: Opening micro-story for healthcare use case
Rebuttals: hosted vs dedicated vs private
Security talking points: SOC 2, KMS, audit logs
Next steps: pilot kickoff & benchmark plan
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-05-21 16:00 UTC | Duration ~62 min | Attendees: Jordan, Riley, Maya, Tom, Priya

[00:00] Jordan: Okay everyone, thanks for joining the pitch kitchen. We're doing a focused run for Acero Health, timing and rebuttals, quick 12-minute demo followed by Q&A rehearsal. Riley, you on deck for the demo?
[00:12] Riley: Yep, I'm on. I want to test the 2-stage narrative: patient triage then internal summarization. We'll call out latency numbers and cost levers, but keep it high level.
[00:25] Maya (muttering): Super, that's what Tom was asking for earlier, like can you show the triage in a minute.
[00:30] Jordan: Cool. Priya, anything specific for security I should weave in?
[00:35] Priya: Yeah, please mention SOC two certificate in the north, um, and KMS integration — and say we have audit logs with per-request metadata. Also call out VPC/private deployment options for PHI, and that we support on-prem/offline packaging.
[00:50] Riley: Noted. I'll say: "For regulated data, we offer private deployment with customer-managed KMS and full audit trails." Try not to say KMS as "kay-em-ess" too often, people glaze over.
[01:04] Jordan: Ha okay. Alright let's run the demo — time me and stop me at the 4, 8, and 12 minute marks.
[01:15] Riley: Starting demo. Screen: demo app, user types: ‘patient complains of chest pain’. Response shows triage priority high and suggested disposition.
[01:33] Riley: (demo) Notice the prefix cache gives us a fast first token, so initial answer on the triage is sub-200ms on p99 in hosted env— um that's generically, ha, that's from our internal bench, caveat.
[01:48] Tom: Quick question, is that number comparable if we go dedicated GPUs?
[01:55] Riley: Good call—dedicated typically lowers variance, p99 drops maybe by 30% depending on GPU and batch. But cost goes up. That's part of the hosted vs dedicated tradeoff.
[02:12] Jordan: [whisper] note: emphasize predictable latency for dedicated.
[02:18] Riley: Next step, internal summarization. We show automatic HPI (history of present illness) extraction, then structured EHR output.
[02:33] Riley: Demo shows a 2 second gen for the summary, though on longer context it could go up.
[02:40] Maya: Can you mention data residency? We have EU patients.
[02:44] Riley: Yes: "You can pin the runtime to a region or run Private for on-prem, we have region controls and data residency options."
[02:55] Jordan: Stop. Time check: 4:02. Okay good, overall pace OK. A couple notes: tighten the health-scare anecdote at the start, it ran long.
[03:10] Jordan: Demo rehearsals tend to drift into technical details — we only want to go deep if asked.
[03:18] Tom: For the security slide, can we have an appendix that lists SOC2 cert date and the KMS providers?
[03:25] Priya: Yes please. Also include pen test cadence and red team reports.
[03:30] Jordan: Action: add appendix slide.
[03:34] Riley: Ok next: we've got a likely objection — "we worry about PHI in hosted API". How do we answer that?
[03:41] Jordan: Script A: "We offer VPC/private deployments and a Private control plane option; for PHI you can opt for on-prem or private VPC with customer-managed encryption keys and HSM support."
[03:53] Priya: Say HSM, customers like that word, it's concrete.
[03:57] Riley: Noted.
[04:02] Jordan: Objection two: "We need predictable unit cost and throughput for scheduled nightly batch runs."
[04:10] Riley: Rebuttal: "Dedicated reserved capacity gives predictable throughput and you can configure autoscaling with burst policies; we also provide per-token costing breakdowns in the Console to model TCO."
[04:24] Maya: Can you give a quick example?
[04:26] Riley: Sure, for a 10k daily job, with dedicated post-quant we estimate X tokens per second per GPU, back-of-envelope cost, and explain batching. (note: we should have a concrete number on slide 9)
[04:40] Jordan: Action: add a worked cost example to slide 9.
[04:45] Riley: Now we'll simulate a procurement question: "What about SLAs and enterprise support?"
[04:52] Jordan: Response: "We offer SLA tiers for Dedicated and Private customers and enterprise support packages, including 24/7 on-call and priority escalation. We'll include an enterprise support addendum."
[05:06] Riley: Sounded fine.
[05:10] Jordan: Time check — 8:00 mark is next. Keep transitions tight.
[05:15] Riley: Moving to failover. If a model variant fails or capacity is constrained, we show automatic fallback to a compatible variant or regional routing. For customers who care about output fidelity we explain fallback quality tradeoffs.
[05:34] Tom: Would we show any benchmark numbers for fallback?
[05:38] Riley: We can show a small table: baseline model p50/p90 vs fallback p50/p90 and mention that fallback is for availability, not quality parity.
[05:48] Jordan: Good. Also mention KV cache and prefix caching to save tokens and preserve latency. But be careful— don't drown them in implementation details. Say: "smart caching reduces cost by X in typical workloads."
[05:59] Riley: Right. 
[06:02] Jordan: All right let's practice some live rebuttal roleplays. Maya, you're the buyer. Tom, you're the technical reviewer, Priya you have tough compliance questions.
[06:12] Maya: Okay, my first objection: "We already use Anthropic for safety — why move?"
[06:18] Riley: Answer: "We don't recommend rip-and-replace, but we provide a predictable inference runtime and cost controls that make it inexpensive to stage a pilot alongside existing providers; plus our model catalog includes open models and integrations with safety tooling."
[06:33] Maya: That was okay, though soundbite about catalogs sounded soft.
[06:38] Jordan: Make the catalog point concrete: 'curated open models + Redwood-verified performance profiles.'
[06:46] Maya: Better. Next: "What about vector DB costs and embeddings?"
[06:50] Riley: Short: "We integrate with major vector providers — Pinecone, Milvus, and also provide first-party embedding endpoints; pricing depends on embedding dimension and retention policies."
[07:05] Tom: Can you not mention Milvus unless the customer asks? We don't want to imply we manage the vector store.
[07:12] Riley: Good note.
[07:15] Jordan: Time check: 12:05. We just ran through the 12 minute cadence. Quick retro: what to cut?
[07:24] Riley: Cut the deep implementation bit on kernel compilation — save for technical deep dives. Keep the demo narrative on observable outcomes.
[07:34] Jordan: Also cut repeated cost math; show one clean worked example and link to spreadsheet.
[07:40] Maya: For the close, can you practice the ask? I want a clear next step.
[07:44] Jordan: Closing script: "If this looks aligned, we'd propose a 6-week pilot: week 0 onboard + two-week validation, week 3 iterate, week 5 production smoke tests. We'll start a joint benchmark and provide a performance spreadsheet."
[07:57] Priya: And include the security checklist and enclave options in the pilot plan.
[08:03] Riley: Roleplay — Maya says she'll need legal to review data flows.
[08:07] Jordan: Response: "We'll share our security pack (SOC2, pen test and architecture diagrams) and an inline mapping of data flows for legal and architecture."
[08:19] Maya: That sounds reasonable.
[08:21] Jordan: We're at 20 minutes into the call — we've still got Q&A practice and a final run. Quick alignment: who owns the appendix slides?
[08:31] Riley: I'll take the appendix: SOC2 cert date, KMS partners, and the quick benchmark table.
[08:36] Jordan: Jordan will craft the closing ask and the pilot timeline.
[08:40] Maya: Tom wants the worked cost example.
[08:44] Tom: Yep.
[08:45] Jordan: Great. Final run: start demo condensed, 3 point narrative, 12 minutes total.
[08:52] Riley: Starting condensed demo... [demo plays; timestamps omitted for clarity] 
[09:30] Riley: Finish demo. Jordan: final 60-second close.
[09:35] Jordan: Close script practiced. Time: 12:03 for the whole run. Good.
[09:42] Priya: One more compliance note: add language about data retention controls — customers like explicit retention windows.
[09:52] Jordan: Add that to appendix.
[09:56] Riley: Last: objections cheat sheet — we should have a single slide with 6 common objections and 1-liner responses.
[10:05] Jordan: Action item for that.
[10:10] Jordan: Okay wrap-up: quick recap and next steps.
[10:15] Jordan: Recap: tighten the opening anecdote, add worked cost example on slide 9, appendix with SOC2/KMS/pen test/retention, cheat sheet slide, and finalize the pilot timeline.
[10:28] Maya: Sounds good. Thank you team.
[10:31] Tom: Thanks.
[10:33] Priya: Thanks all.

Note: transcription includes slight mis-hearings (SOC two, kay-em-ess), and occasional speaker attribution uncertainty typical of call transcripts.
